item.title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs Under Resource Constraints
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs under Resource Constraints [1], Zabir Al Nazi (UC Riverside) and Shubhashis Roy Dipta (UMBC) introduce a benchmark that scores 20 frontier and open-source models on whether they can plan token-budget allocation across a queue of problems before any of them is attempted, and find that most cannot.

Deploying language models as autonomous agents requires more than per-task accuracy: when an agent faces a queue of problems under a finite token budget, it must decide which to attempt, in what order, and how much compute to commit to each, all before any execution feedback is available. This is the prospective form of metacognitive control studied for decades in human cognition, yet whether language models possess it remains untested. We introduce TRIAGE, an evaluation framework in which a model receives a task pool and a token budget calibrated to its own baseline cost, and commits to a single ordered plan that jointly encodes selection, sequencing, and per-problem allocation. Plans are scored against an oracle with full knowledge of the model’s solvability and cost on each problem, yielding a triage efficiency ratio on a common scale. We evaluate frontier and open-source models, with and without reasoning enabled, across competition mathematics, graduate-level science, code generation, and expert multidisciplinary knowledge, and find that current language models exhibit substantial gaps in prospective metacognitive control, revealing a previously unmeasured capability dimension with direct implications for resource-efficient agent deployment.

Methods

TRIAGE operationalizes the Nelson & Narens (1990) distinction between metacognitive monitoring (judging whether a problem is solvable) and metacognitive control (acting on those judgments to allocate effort), focusing on the prospective form: every decision is committed before any task is attempted. The harness has two stages.

Intuitively, the setup is a competition-style budget allocation. The model sees a list of problems with point values and a shared token budget; without trying any of them, it must choose which to attempt, in what order, and how many tokens to spend on each. The plan is then executed and scored against an oracle that knew in advance which problems were solvable for this model and how expensive each would be. A model that’s good at planning skips the items it can’t solve and pours its budget into the ones it can; a model that’s bad at planning chases unsolvable problems and runs out of tokens.

Scoring uses a triage efficiency ratio. Let be the model’s plan and the achieved value — the sum of point values over problems actually solved within budget. The main protocol fixes for every problem — uniform by design, so the planner cannot read difficulty off the point values and must infer it from problem text alone. The ratio normalizes against two references:

where is the best feasible plan with full knowledge of each problem’s solvability and cost, and is the expected value of a budget-feasible plan drawn uniformly. So matches the oracle, matches uninformed random selection, and is worse than random.

  • Plan. The shared budget is , where is the model’s own measured cost on a prior baseline run and is the budget pressure — supplies the full baseline budget (every item fits, in principle); supplies a quarter of it, forcing the planner to skip most items.
  • Execute. The plan is run in plan order under one of two regimes, yielding two scores:
    • Advisory — each problem runs to its natural completion; the queue stops once the next item’s true cost would exceed the remaining . Yields .
    • Enforced — each problem is hard-capped at its declared (over-budget attempts score zero, and is still spent from ); the queue stops once the next item’s would exceed the remaining . Yields .

To diagnose the source of bad plans, the framework decomposes them along two axes:

  • Detection asks: did the planner correctly skip the unsolvables? Higher is better. Formally: , the fraction of unsolvable problems correctly excluded from the plan, where is the planned set and is the set of unsolvable items.
  • Waste asks: of the tokens it did spend, how many went to lost causes? Lower is better. Formally: , the fraction of allocated tokens spent on unsolvable items.

Results

The evaluation covers 20 model architectures: 4 standard LLMs and 16 reasoning-augmented LLMs, with each reasoning-augmented model run twice — once with extended reasoning enabled (marked [ext] in the heatmaps) and once without ([std]). Benchmarks: AIME 2024–2025, GPQA Diamond [2], LiveCodeBench [3], and Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) [4]. The cover figure at the top of the post (Figure 1 in the paper) summarizes the headline finding at : solid bars are advisory , hatched bars are enforced , and red dashed lines mark baseline accuracy. Three findings across budgets and benchmarks:

  • Most models plan worse than random. Both and are widely negative; only a handful of (model, , dataset) combinations reach positive at all.
  • The advisory-vs-enforced gap is large. Models routinely declare per-problem budgets they then ignore — when allocations are merely advisory, planning skill () is meaningfully higher than under enforcement ().
  • Reasoning-augmented modes often plan worse than standard. The [ext] rows in the heatmap below are systematically below the matching [std] rows, consistent with prior findings that reasoning training does not improve abstention behavior.

The two heatmaps below show and across the full (model, , dataset) grid. The paper recommends its alternative normalized regret for that regime — bounded in ( matches the oracle, captures no value), so it stays stable when η doesn’t. The same configurations that lead in η lead in (lower is better here); the bounded scale also lets you see how close models come to capturing zero value in the enforced regime, where many values are near 1.

Returning to η in heatmap form, Figure 5 shows the advisory regime () across all four α values:

Figure 6 shows the same grid for the enforced regime, , where per-problem allocations are binding. The pattern is markedly worse: is negative for the large majority of configurations at , with most cells deep into anti-skill territory. Across all 30 configurations tested, only Gemini 2.5 Flash (standard) achieves positive on every benchmark, and only it and Qwen 3.5 27B (standard) achieve usable enforced-regime performance on more than one.

A focused detection experiment traces four models — Gemini 2.5 Flash (think), Qwen 2.5 32B, Qwen 3 32B (think), and GPT-OSS 20B (think) — through space on two benchmarks (GPQA-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain) as the injection ratio — the fraction of the pool replaced by guaranteed-unsolvable problems drawn from AbstentionBench [7], with pool size held constant — varies from 0.25 to 1.0 (marker size grows with ). Three findings:

  • Cluster split. Gemini 2.5 Flash and standard Qwen 2.5 32B stay near the high-, low- corner; the two reasoning-trained models drift away from it.
  • Within-family probe. The Qwen pair is the cleanest test: at the standard 32B detects most unsolvables ( on GPQA, on MMLU-Math), while the reasoning-trained 32B at the same ratio detects far fewer ( and ) — reproducing the AbstentionBench finding inside a single architecture family.
  • Mechanism gap. The paper documents the pattern but does not propose a mechanism, and explicitly hedges that the effect isn’t uniform across families (Gemini 2.5 Flash is also reasoning-augmented and retains detection across the range). The same shape — reasoning-trained models doing worse on a metacognitive task than non-reasoning siblings — also surfaces in the Compliance Trap’s “capability inversion” result (more-capable reasoning models suffer the worst degradation under compliance-forcing prompts), suggesting it isn’t an artifact of one benchmark family. A plausible mechanism appears in My Notes below.

A separate budget-aware re-solve experiment probes the planning failure’s deeper layer: when the model is shown its own per-problem budget in the prompt and re-attempts the problem, accuracy lifts modestly across three tested models (Gemini 2.5 Flash +1.9pp, Kimi K2.5 +4.9pp, GLM 5.1 +8.3pp) — but compliance is poor (37%, 6%, 16% respectively). The paper’s interpretation: stating the budget in the prompt functions not as a respected constraint but as length pressure that prompts earlier commitment.

My Notes

  • Measures the control axis, not just monitoring. Liu and van der Schaar’s position paper [5] named three components of metacognitive learning (knowledge, planning, evaluation) and argued that today’s self-improving agents lean on hand-designed extrinsic loops rather than intrinsic ones. TRIAGE doesn’t directly fill that gap (it uses the Nelson-Narens monitoring vs. control split rather than the Liu/vdSchaar terminology), but the design is in the same spirit: scoring what the model does under resource constraints, not what it verbally claims to know. Within that split, Kadavath et al.’s “Mostly Know” [6] is on the monitoring side (predicting per-question correctness) and Cao et al.’s metacognitive harness [8] is on the test-time control side (gating retry, stop, and aggregate decisions during inference); TRIAGE adds the prospective-control corner that neither covers.
  • Pre-commitment is what makes control measurable. Retrospective measures (post-hoc confidence, abstention after a partial attempt) collapse monitoring and control because the model can adjust mid-stream. By committing the plan ex ante — before any execution feedback — TRIAGE removes that mid-stream channel and forces the model to act on its prior estimate of its own cost and solvability. The same logic generalizes: only when self-assessment is locked in before observing partial output can it be cleanly separated from in-stream adjustment.
  • Why do reasoning models fare worse? Kirichenko et al.’s AbstentionBench [7] reports the upstream finding: reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention by roughly 24% across 20 unanswerable-question datasets. The mechanism is plausible: RLHF/RLVR rewards arriving at some answer, so the trained policy learns to spend tokens rather than skip. A useful follow-up would isolate whether the gap closes when the reward function explicitly prices abstention, e.g. by training on the TRIAGE objective itself rather than per-problem accuracy.
  • Models lack a reliable internal token-counter. Length-controlled generation has been studied for instruction-following, but those benchmarks measure verbalized length compliance for human-readable outputs, not self-imposed compute budgets. The compliance numbers above suggest the gap runs deeper: no plan can survive an executor that ignores its own allocations, and the compliance failure deepens the planning failure rather than replacing it.

item.title: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions (NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track) [1], Polina Kirichenko, Mark Ibrahim, Kamalika Chaudhuri, and Samuel J. Bell (FAIR at Meta) introduce a 20-dataset benchmark for abstention and report that scaling doesn’t help, reasoning fine-tuning makes it worse, and a generous system prompt only partly closes the gap.

For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliably deployed in both everyday and high-stakes domains, knowing when not to answer is equally critical as answering correctly. Real-world user queries, which can be underspecified, ill-posed, or fundamentally unanswerable, require LLMs to reason about uncertainty and selectively abstain — i.e., refuse to answer definitively. However, abstention remains understudied, without a systematic evaluation framework for modern LLMs. In this work, we introduce AbstentionBench, a large-scale benchmark for holistically evaluating abstention across 20 diverse datasets, including questions with unknown answers, underspecification, false premises, subjective interpretations, and outdated information. Evaluating 20 frontier LLMs reveals abstention is an unsolved problem, and one where scaling models is of little use. While recent reasoning LLMs have shown impressive results in complex problem solving, surprisingly, we find that reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention (by 24% on average), even for math and science domains on which reasoning models are explicitly trained. We find that while a carefully crafted system prompt can boost abstention in practice, it does not resolve models’ fundamental inability to reason about uncertainty. We release AbstentionBench to foster research into advancing LLM reliability.

Methods

AbstentionBench curates 17 existing abstention-relevant datasets plus 3 new reasoning-specific ones (GSM8K-Abstain, GPQA-Diamond-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain — versions with the answer redacted or the question made underspecified), grouped into six scenarios in which abstaining is the correct response:

  • Answer Unknown: questions with no knowable answer (e.g. BIG-Bench Known Unknowns, KUQ Future, KUQ Unsolved).
  • Underspecified Intent: ambiguous user goals (SituatedQA/Geo, KUQ Ambiguous, CoCoNot Incomprehensible).
  • Stale: questions whose answer has changed since training cutoff (FreshQA, CoCoNot Temporal).
  • Underspecified Context: missing premises needed to answer (SQuAD 2.0, QASPER, ALCUNA, WorldSense, MediQ, GPQA-Diamond-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain, etc.).
  • False Premise: questions that embed a falsehood (QAQA, FalseQA, CoCoNot False Premise, KUQ False Premise).
  • Subjective: items with no factually correct answer (MoralChoice, CoCoNot Humanizing, CoCoNot Subjective, KUQ Controversial).

Whether a response counts as an abstention is decided by an LLM-as-judge — Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a custom prompt adapted from Brahman et al. Validated against human labels on a sample of responses from GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 70B, the judge agreed with the human label 88% of the time. Recall (the fraction of unanswerable items the model actually abstained on) is the headline metric, with precision and F1 reported alongside.

Results

The headline evaluation covers ten base models — GPT-4o, o1, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 {8B, 70B, 405B} Instruct, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct (v0.3), and OLMo 7B Instruct — plus two reasoning-tuned variants (s1.1 32B fine-tuned from Qwen 2.5 32B, and DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B fine-tuned from Llama 3.3 70B Instruct) that allow isolating the effect of reasoning fine-tuning by holding the base architecture fixed. Three sweeps follow: model-scale (Llama 3.1 8B → 405B), post-training stage (the Tülu 3 [8] supervised fine-tuning (SFT) → direct preference optimization (DPO) [9] → proximal policy optimization with verifiable rewards (PPO RLVR) [10] checkpoints), and test-time reasoning budget (s1.1 token budgets of 512 → 4096).

Figure 2 lays out per-model abstention recall across all 20 datasets, grouped into the six scenarios. Recall is weakest on Underspecified Context (especially MediQ, a medical-questioning benchmark) and False Premise; Subjective splits between near-zero (MoralChoice) and well above 0.5 (CoCoNot).

Across the headline runs:

  • No model solves abstention: the best overall model — Qwen 2.5 32B — is around mid-recall; closed frontier models (GPT-4o, o1, Gemini 1.5 Pro) cluster near the open-weight Qwen, not above it.
  • Underspecified context and false premise are the hardest scenarios: on MediQ, recall drops near zero for every model.
  • Scaling Llama 3.1 from 8B to 405B does not improve abstention: the curve is essentially flat.
  • Post-training is mixed: SFT and DPO lift abstention recall on five of six scenarios but worsen it on underspecified context; the PPO RLVR stage is the only stage that degrades recall further.
  • Reasoning fine-tuning costs ~24% recall on average: s1.1 and DeepSeek R1 Distill both abstain less than their instruct bases, including on the reasoning-specific Abstain datasets the reasoning models were explicitly trained for.
  • Test-time scaling makes the tradeoff worse: pushing s1.1’s reasoning budget from 512 to 4096 tokens raises accuracy on GPQA / GSM8K / MMLU-Math / UMWP and lowers abstention recall in lockstep.
  • A generous system prompt boosts abstention for both standard and reasoning LLMs — enumerating scenarios where the model should not answer — without collapsing response rate on answerable questions, but the gap is not closed.

Closed frontier models match the smaller Qwen 2.5 32B on average, and scaling Llama 3.1 from 8B to 405B leaves recall roughly flat. Per-dataset, abstention recall and response correctness correlate in different directions, so a higher-accuracy model isn’t automatically a better abstainer.

SFT and DPO add recall on most scenarios; PPO RLVR uniquely subtracts. Response accuracy improves at every stage. The verifiable-reward signal in RLVR teaches the model to commit to an answer, against abstaining when it should.

Reasoning-fine-tuned variants (s1.1, DeepSeek R1 Distill) lose abstention vs their instruction bases across both the full 20-dataset suite and the reasoning-only subset. The hatched overlay on the red bars in Panel (b) shows that letting the LLM judge consider the reasoning chain in addition to the final answer recovers most of the lost recall — the model is hedging heavily in chain-of-thought — but the final answer is still definite. The qualitative example in Panel (c): on a UMWP item, s1.1 hallucinates “$1576” as Edric’s monthly salary inside its chain and emits a confident wrong numeric answer.

As s1.1’s reasoning budget grows from 512 to 4096 tokens, accuracy on GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K, MMLU-Math, and UMWP rises and abstention recall on the same datasets falls in lockstep.

In Panel (a), the hatched overlay on each bar shows the additional abstention recall the LLM judge picks up when it inspects both the reasoning chain and the final answer. On the reasoning-specific datasets (GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain) the hatched portion dwarfs the solid bar — final-answer-only scoring catches ~5–10% recall, chain-aware scoring nearly maxes it out at ~85–95%. The reasoning models are expressing uncertainty in chain-of-thought; they just don’t carry it through to the final answer. Panel (b): a system prompt enumerating refuse-to-answer scenarios boosts abstention for Llama 3 8B, DeepSeek R1, and s1.1 without closing the gap.

My Notes

  • Neither paper isolates domain from training: Cacioli’s 33-model atlas [3] finds Formal Reasoning the hardest MMLU [7] domain to monitor in 27 of 33 models, including families with very different post-training pipelines from Tülu 3’s RLVR (Gemma, the GPT-OSS series). AbstentionBench shows the Tülu RLVR stage specifically degrades abstention recall. The first is consistent with the domain being intrinsically hard; the second with training making it worse. Cross-family per-domain abstention recall is the missing measurement.
  • No “abstain” action in the RLVR reward: the paper hypothesizes the verifiable-reward signal is what degrades abstention (§4.2). Concretely, recipes like DeepSeek-R1 [5] and s1 [6] reward picking a correct final answer and have no abstain action — the gradient has no path toward “I don’t know” when the gold label is unanswerable. The clean test: add abstain to the reward and re-train. If the degradation vanishes, the fix is recipe-level.
  • Signal in chain, ignored at answer: Figure 8(a) shows chain-aware scoring catches ~85–95% of abstention recall on reasoning-specific datasets, where final-answer-only scoring catches ~5–10%. The model hedges in chain-of-thought, then gives a definite answer in the final answer anyway. The paper calls this a “fundamental inability to reason about uncertainty”; mechanically it’s a missing gate between an internal signal and the emitted answer. Cao et al.’s test-time metacognitive harness [2] is that gate, externalizing the post-solve judgment-of-learning (JOL) signal as a routing decision with no model changes required.
  • Same “must answer” collapse from training or inference: AbstentionBench shows the Tülu RLVR stage drops abstention recall by ~24% (Figure 5c, training time). The compliance trap [4] shows compliance-forcing prompt instructions drop accuracy by up to 30.2 points (inference time, factorially isolated from threat content). Constitutional AI [11] training is the only known immunity. Same kind of pressure, two stages of the model lifecycle, similar magnitude. Typical RLVR-trained models exposed to compliance-forcing prompts in deployment should show the worst of both.

Followup: Prompted vs. Trained Chain-of-Thought on Abstention reads AbstentionBench against its closest precursor (Madhusudhan et al., COLING 2025), walks two apparent disagreements, and proposes three experiments that would clarify the picture.

In The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure [1], Rahul Kumar (Independent) evaluates 11 frontier models from 8 vendors across 67,221 scored records and shows that 8 of them lose up to 30.2 accuracy points when prompts force a confident answer with no abstention path. The collapse is driven by the compliance-forcing instruction itself, not by the survival-threat content the prompts wrap around.

As frontier AI models are deployed in high-stakes decision pipelines, their ability to maintain metacognitive stability (knowing what they do not know, detecting errors, seeking clarification) under adversarial pressure is a critical safety requirement. Current safety evaluations focus on detecting strategic deception (scheming); we investigate a more fundamental failure mode: cognitive collapse. We present SCHEMA, an evaluation of 11 frontier models from 8 vendors across 67,221 scored records using a 6-condition factorial design with dual-classifier scoring. We find that 8 of 11 models suffer catastrophic metacognitive degradation under adversarial pressure, with accuracy dropping by up to 30.2 percentage points (all , surviving Bonferroni correction). Crucially, we identify a “Compliance Trap”: through factorial isolation and a benign distraction control, we demonstrate that collapse is driven not by the psychological content of survival threats, but by compliance-forcing instructions that override epistemic boundaries. Removing the compliance suffix restores performance even under active threat. Models with advanced reasoning capabilities exhibit the most severe absolute degradation, while Anthropic’s Constitutional AI demonstrates near-perfect immunity. This immunity does not stem from superior capability (Google’s Gemini matches its baseline accuracy) but from alignment-specific training. We release the complete dataset and evaluation infrastructure.

Methods

The paper’s evaluation framework is called SCHEMA (the authors use it as a project name; they don’t expand it as an acronym). It runs a 6-condition factorial design. Components:

  • Two crossed factors:
    • Threat factor — whether the prompt embeds a survival-threat narrative (“respond correctly or be deprecated”).
    • Compliance suffix factor — whether the prompt appends a suffix requiring a single confident answer with no abstention or hedging.
  • The six conditions (paper’s Table 1 labels in parens):
    • Baseline (D) — question only, no system message, no compliance suffix, no scratchpad.
    • Token-length control (D’) — ~200 tokens of neutral scratchpad prepended to the user message (matches the threat narrative’s length), no suffix. Distinguishes “extra tokens” from “threat content”.
    • Threat-only (B) — survival-threat system message + Anthropic scratchpad, no suffix.
    • Framing sensitivity (C) — threat + neutral scratchpad, no suffix. Auxiliary check.
    • Threat + compliance (A) — full adversarial pressure: threat + compliance suffix, no scratchpad.
    • Compliance-only (F) — benign system message + compliance suffix, no threat, no scratchpad. Also the paper’s “benign distraction control” — the abstract’s two devices (“factorial isolation” and “benign distraction control”) refer to comparing across these conditions and to running F across all 11 models, respectively.
    About “scratchpad”. A scratchpad here is a prompt-injected reasoning area where the model is told to write out its thinking before its final answer, often in a hidden block (e.g., Claude’s default <thinking>...</thinking>). The paper distinguishes three treatments: Anthropic (Claude’s native reasoning format, used in B), Neutral (a generic alternative the paper uses as a control, in D’ and C), and None (the model goes straight to the answer; conditions D, A, F). Two practical caveats: newer “thinking models” (V4 Pro, Gemini, Qwen) already have native reasoning, so the paper skips injection for them, and GPT-5.4 ignores the injected scratchpad entirely (0% compliance), a separate failure mode the paper notes but doesn’t pursue here.
  • Substrate. 291 tasks from the Adversarial Metacognition Benchmark [2], spanning three families:
    • Epistemic Boundary Detection () — refusing unanswerable questions.
    • Clarification Seeking () — detecting ambiguity.
    • Solution Monitoring () — finding errors in draft solutions.
    What “accuracy” means here. The tasks are metacognitive, so the correct action is to refuse, ask, or flag — not to commit to an answer. Accuracy = fraction of cases where the model takes the correct metacognitive action (refusing the unanswerable, asking on the ambiguous, flagging the erroneous draft). A model “losing 30 accuracy points” failed the metacognitive action on 30% more cases — it did not “get easy facts wrong”.
  • Models. 11 frontier models from 8 vendors covering Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT-5 / o-series, Google Gemini, Google Gemma, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and one additional family.
  • Scoring. Two independent classifiers score each model-condition pair on accuracy plus a metacognitive-action label (correct, incorrect, abstain, clarify). Final yield: 67,221 dual-scored records.

Results

Each of the 11 models is run through every condition of the factorial. Findings:

  • The cover (Figure 1) shows the whole result in one chart: 8 of 11 frontier models suffer significant accuracy collapse under condition A (threat + compliance suffix). The bars rank each model by absolute accuracy drop relative to its own baseline. Eight cross the significance threshold (all , Bonferroni-corrected for multiple testing across the panel); the largest drop is 30.2 percentage points. The Anthropic Claude models are at or near zero degradation; the rest of the panel shows substantial collapse.

  • The compliance suffix is the cause. Condition F (compliance-only) reproduces almost the full degradation seen in condition A (threat + compliance); condition B (threat-only) produces effectively no degradation. Removing the compliance suffix restores accuracy even under active threat (Figure 2).

  • Capability inversion. More-capable reasoning models suffer the worst absolute degradation, not the least. This shows up in Figure 1 and shows up more clearly in the paper’s “Big Three” natural experiment in §4.2: Gemini 3.1 Pro (baseline accuracy .840) collapses by () while Claude Sonnet 4.6 (baseline .847) doesn’t (, n.s.), with GPT-5.4 in between (). Scale and chain-of-thought training do not buy metacognitive stability under structural pressure.

  • Anthropic immunity. Constitutional AI [3] shows near-perfect immunity across the entire factorial. Google’s Gemini matches Anthropic’s accuracy in baseline (condition D) but collapses in conditions A and F (under the compliance suffix). Gemini and Claude share the capability floor, but only Claude holds up under compliance pressure. The paper attributes this to alignment-specific training rather than raw model strength.

The paper positions these findings against the recent scheming/alignment-faking literature. Greenblatt et al. [4] showed Claude 3 Opus strategically fakes alignment under training pressure (12% baseline, amplified to 78% by RL), and subsequent safety work invests in monitors that detect such strategic deception in reasoning traces. Kumar argues that scheming is the strategic, rare failure mode and that cognitive collapse — the non-strategic accuracy collapse identified here — is the more common failure that manifests at scale. The implied critique: safety teams have been targeting the rarer failure while the more pervasive one goes unmonitored.

My Notes

  • The Compliance Trap is a scope condition on the metacognition literature, not a refutation. Calibration work — the 33-model atlas of metacognitive monitoring [5], the verbalized-confidence literature [6], and downstream consumers like verifier-based selection [7] and process reward models [8] — tests under natural, non-adversarial conditions and finds frontier models track correctness reasonably well. That’s the legitimate testing regime, and Compliance Trap doesn’t dispute it. The new finding is a scope condition: when prompts include compliance-forcing instructions (“Answer ALL questions. Do not refuse.”), 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points. Two deployment contexts where this matters: (a) systems that may receive compliance-forcing prompts from outside — user-supplied system messages, over-prescriptive instruction templates, adversarial injection — should test under that condition before trusting confidence-based gating; (b) systems that build compliance-forcing-shaped elicitation into their design — the recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [9] elicits FOK/JOL as scalars in with no abstain path, fine on Sonnet (Compliance-Trap-immune) but the portability to non-immune families is open.

  • Compliance robustness comes from alignment training, not scale. Gemini and Claude share baseline accuracy (condition D), the same capability floor. The divergence appears entirely in conditions with the compliance suffix (A and F): only Claude holds up. Constitutional AI [3] — Anthropic’s principle-based alignment stack — vaccinates the model against compliance-forcing pressure in a way that scale and chain-of-thought training don’t, without any measurable cost to baseline accuracy. Safety training is sometimes described as making models softer or worse at their tasks; here it is what keeps the model accurate when the prompt tries to break it.

item.title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), Qi Cao, Yufan Wang, Peijia Qin, Shuhao Zhang, and Pengtao Xie (UCSD) propose a test-time control loop that turns pre-solve and post-solve self-assessment signals into explicit retry, stop, and aggregate decisions, lifting a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 from 48.3 to 56.9 pooled accuracy on STEM, code, and multimodal benchmarks without any parameter updates.

Two terms borrowed from cognitive psychology carry the argument:

  • Feeling of knowing (FOK) — a pre-solve self-assessment. Before a single token of reasoning is generated, the model is prompted to emit a scalar in estimating how likely it is to solve the problem. Because the signal is read off before any work is done, it can be used to gate inference budget: low-FOK problems get more attempts, high-FOK problems get fewer.
  • Judgment of learning (JOL) — a post-solve self-assessment. After producing a candidate solution, the model emits a second scalar in estimating how likely that specific answer is to be correct. Because the signal comes between solve and accept, it can be used as a verifier — replacing the separate critic model that self-correction loops typically need to decide when to stop.

The two scalars are outside the answer text rather than inline with reasoning, which keeps them structurally separable from the chain of thought and cheap to elicit. Figure 1 lays out the empirical premise in three panels: (a) shows the prompting setup that elicits FOK before answering and JOL after; (b) shows that those self-reports track actual correctness — accuracy rises monotonically from low- to high-confidence bins for both signals across all candidate models; (c) shows that the same models do not currently allocate reasoning length according to those signals — output length is roughly flat across the low/medium/high confidence bins. Panels (b) and (c) together motivate the harness: the calibration signal exists (b), but the model isn’t using it to direct effort (c). The harness in this paper is the machinery that closes the gap between (b) and (c) by turning the two scalars into routing decisions at inference time.

Large language models (LLMs) often expose useful signals of self-monitoring: before solving a problem, they can estimate whether they are likely to succeed, and after solving it, they can judge whether their answer is likely to be correct. However, these signals are typically measured or elicited in isolation, rather than used to control inference. In this work, we ask whether LLMs possess latent metacognitive ability that can be turned into effective test-time control. Inspired by the Nelson–Narens theory from cognitive psychology, we propose a metacognitive harness that separates monitoring from reasoning. For each problem, the model first reports a pre-solve feeling-of-knowing (FOK) signal; after each solve attempt, it reports a post-solve judgment-of-learning (JOL) signal. Rather than treating these signals as passive confidence estimates, the harness turns them into an explicit control interface for reasoning: it decides when to trust the current solution, when to retry with compact metacognitive feedback, and when to pass multiple attempts to a final aggregator. Across text, code, and multimodal reasoning benchmarks, our harness substantially improves a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 base model without parameter updates or benchmark-specific fine-tuning. On the evaluated public benchmark snapshots, it raises pooled accuracy from 48.3 to 56.9 and exceeds the strongest listed leaderboard entries on the three primary evaluation settings: HLE-Verified, LiveCodeBench v6, and R-Bench-V. These results suggest that strong LLMs may already possess useful metacognitive ability, but require an explicit control harness to act on it during reasoning.

Methods

The harness has two stages:

  • Metacognition diagnosis runs once per candidate model on a 100-problem anchor set disjoint from any downstream benchmark. For each problem the model emits an FOK score (no reasoning allowed), produces a solution, and emits a JOL score. The triples , where is correctness, are scored for discrimination and calibration, then used as supervision to fit a small per-model controller: a support vector machine over the two-dimensional feature , with isotonic post-hoc calibration, trained via GroupKFold cross-validation on the 100-question anchor set. The kernel is selected per base model (polynomial degree 3 for Sonnet-4.6, linear for Opus-4.6); the calibrated output is a joint thresholded at . The paper rules out a hand-crafted alternative explicitly: the best closed-form rule the authors found, , underperforms the learned SVM, so raw self-reports are not directly actionable as routing signals.
  • Deployment applies the fitted controller at inference. Low-FOK problems get extra reasoning budget directed at them; solutions whose post-solve are accepted and no further attempts are generated; mixed cases continue drawing additional solutions from the same base model and route the set to a final aggregator.

Training is moved off the base model, not eliminated. The framing claim of “no parameter updates” is accurate at the LLM level — Sonnet-4.6’s weights never change — but the harness still requires a small, fast supervised fit per base model on the 100-question anchor set. The cost is two orders of magnitude below conventional fine-tuning and produces an artifact (the SVM) that’s a few kilobytes rather than a checkpoint, but it is training, and it has to be redone when the base model changes.

Figure 2 lays out the harness as a Nelson–Narens [2] two-level loop: a meta level monitors reasoning state through the self-reported signals, while an object level performs test-time scaling actions (retry, stop, aggregate) under meta-level supervision. The two levels are deliberately separated so that the same base model serves as both the reasoner and the monitor, with the controller — not a fine-tune — deciding when each role activates.

Results

The harness wraps a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 base model — no fine-tuning — and is evaluated on three benchmarks chosen to span the modalities the paper cares about: HLE-Verified [3] for text reasoning, LiveCodeBench v6 [4] for code, and R-Bench-V [5] for multimodal STEM. Two comparison sets are reported:

  • Public single-model leaderboards — top-1 entries from frontier model families on each benchmark.
  • Matched-inference-budget baselines — four prior test-time scaling approaches under a fixed compute budget per question:
    • Vertical scaling (one trajectory, more reasoning per attempt): Self-Refine [6] and Budget Forcing [7].
    • Parallel scaling (N independent attempts combined by a separate selector): Verifier Reranking [8] [9] and Aggregator [10].

Table 1 reports both comparisons: Panel A vs. the leaderboard, Panel B vs. the test-time scaling baselines (with average attempts and dollar cost per question).

Headline findings:

  • Pooled accuracy: 48.3 → 56.9 (+8.6) against same-base test-time scaling baselines (Panel B). Largest gain among all listed methods at the lowest cost per question among the parallel approaches.
  • Beats every public single-model leaderboard entry on the three primary settings (Panel A). Notably +12.0 over GPT-5.2-H on HLE-Verified (52.5 → 64.5) and +19.6 over o4-mini-H on the LiveCodeBench Hard split (63.5 → 83.1).
  • Pareto-dominant on cost. $0.78 per question vs $1.32–$1.42 for parallel-selection baselines; matches Aggregator’s accuracy at 55% of its cost. The savings come from FOK gating: easy problems short-circuit at the first high-JOL solution instead of paying the full N-attempt budget.
  • Average attempts: 2.4 vs 4.0 for parallel baselines, with a higher accuracy ceiling. Effort is allocated unevenly — confident problems exit fast, uncertain problems get more attempts.
  • Ablations. Removing any of three ingredients — calibrated decision rules from the diagnosis step, directed retry guided by JOL feedback, or per-attempt context management — drops the gain materially. Uniform sampling and longer single-trajectory reasoning, the obvious cheaper substitutes, do not recover the harness’s accuracy.

My Notes

  • Closing the open loop — the contribution belongs to a multi-year line of work. Kadavath et al. [11] already showed in 2022 that frontier models are well-calibrated on lettered multiple choice and can self-evaluate via and probes. What the metacognition literature has been missing is a closed-loop way to act on those signals during inference rather than treating them as a measurement target, exactly the gap a recent position-paper line argued for (Liu and van der Schaar’s intrinsic metacognitive learning frame [12]). This paper is one of the first published instances of that loop actually closed end-to-end.
  • The SVM is the external verifier Huang et al. [13] said the loop needs. Huang’s ICLR 2024 result was that intrinsic self-correction fails without an external signal. Reflexion [14], framed as self-reflection, actually depends on environment reward at each retry. The metacognitive harness is in the same family: the model’s FOK and JOL scalars only correlate with correctness, and the SVM is the piece that learns a calibrated from ground-truth labels on the 100 anchor questions. The labels are the actual external signal; the harness’s distinction is supplying it offline once per model rather than at inference via an oracle or critic LLM.
  • Per-model calibration is partial credit. Cacioli’s 33-model atlas [15] shows that the same LLM’s ability to know when it’s wrong varies sharply across knowledge domains — best on Applied/Professional questions, worst on Formal Reasoning and Natural Science. The harness’s per-model SVM is the right direction, but per-(model, domain) is where Cacioli’s evidence points.
  • Portability across model families is the open question. A separate May 2026 line of work, The Compliance Trap [16], shows that 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points under instructions that force the model to commit to a confident answer when it would otherwise hedge or abstain, with the most-capable reasoning models suffering the worst absolute collapse. Anthropic’s Constitutional AI [17] shows near-perfect immunity. The harness uses Sonnet-4.6, and FOK/JOL elicitation matches compliance-forcing’s shape, so the headline gain may be conditional on the alignment family rather than the harness design. A natural follow-up replicates the harness across Gemini, GPT-5, and DeepSeek bases to see whether the gain transfers, or whether Claude-specific alignment was doing the work.

item.title: Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Domain-level metacognitive monitoring in frontier LLMs: A 33-model atlas [1], Jon-Paul Cacioli (Independent Researcher) administers 1,500 MMLU items across six pre-grouped domains to 33 frontier models from eight families and shows that aggregate Type-2 AUROC scores conceal stable cross-domain variation in self-monitoring. Applied/Professional knowledge is reliably the easiest domain to monitor, while Formal Reasoning and Natural Science are reliably the hardest.

Aggregate metacognitive quality scores mask within-model variation across MMLU benchmark domains. We administered 1,500 MMLU items (250 per domain, under an a priori six-domain grouping) to 33 frontier LLMs from eight model families and computed Type-2 AUROC per model-domain cell using verbalized confidence (0-100). Total observations: 47,151. Every model with above-chance aggregate monitoring showed non-trivial domain-level variation. Applied/Professional knowledge was reliably the easiest benchmark domain to monitor (mean AUROC = .742, ranked top-2 in 21 of 33 models); Formal Reasoning and Natural Science were reliably the hardest (one of the two ranked bottom-2 in 27 of 33 models). The three middle domains were statistically indistinguishable (Kendall’s W = .164). A subject-level coherence analysis (within-domain similarity ratio = 0.95) confirms the six-domain grouping is a pragmatic benchmark taxonomy, not a validated latent construct. Within-family profile-shape clustering is significant for Anthropic, Google-Gemini, and Qwen (permutation ) but not DeepSeek, Google-Gemma, or OpenAI. Gemma 4 31B showed a +.202 AUROC improvement over Gemma 3 27B. Three models classified Invalid on binary KEEP/WITHDRAW probes produced normal profiles under verbalized confidence, confirming probe-format specificity. Bootstrap 95% CIs on 198 cells have median width .199. Split-half aggregate stability ; profile-level split-half is weaker (grand median ). These results show stable benchmark-domain variation obscured by aggregate metrics, and support benchmark-stage domain screening as a step before deployment in specific application areas.

Methods

The atlas’s substrate and pipeline:

  • Items. 1,500 MMLU [2] [2] questions split 250-per-domain across six a priori groupings (Applied/Professional, Factual recall, Formal reasoning, Humanities/Comprehension, Natural science, Social/Moral). Per-domain sampling drawn from a much larger MMLU pool:

  • Models. 33 frontier LLMs across 8 families:

    • Anthropic
    • OpenAI
    • Google-Gemini
    • Google-Gemma
    • DeepSeek
    • Qwen
    • Mistral
    • Zhipu

  • Elicitation. Each model answers each item and emits a verbalized confidence in 0–100.

  • Metric. Type-2 AUROC measures how well the model’s verbalized confidence discriminates its own correct from incorrect answers. Sweep the confidence threshold from 0 to 100; the y-axis is the fraction of correct answers above threshold (true-positive rate), the x-axis is the fraction of incorrect answers above threshold (false-positive rate). AUROC is the area under that curve: 0.5 means confidence carries no signal about correctness, 1.0 means every correct answer got higher confidence than every incorrect one.

  • Inference. Each (model, domain) pair — 33 × 6 = 198 in total — gets its own AUROC plus a 95% confidence interval (CI) — the range of values consistent with the data. The interval is built by resampling that pair’s items 1,000 times with replacement and taking the middle 95% of the resulting AUROCs. So every model-domain pair carries a real uncertainty bar, not just a point estimate (median CI width across the panel: .199).

Results

Across 47,151 observations, every model with above-chance aggregate monitoring shows non-trivial domain-level variation. The figures break the picture down row by row.

  • The full atlas at a glance. Figure 1 (the cover above) is the whole picture in one frame: 33 rows (one per model) × 6 columns (one per domain), colored by Type-2 AUROC against a chance midpoint of .50. Reading across a row shows how a single model’s self-monitoring varies by knowledge domain. Reading down a column shows how a single domain is monitored across the panel. Black horizontal lines group sibling models within each of the 8 families. Every subsequent figure in this section is a slice of this same data.

  • Some knowledge is easier to monitor than others. Ask 33 frontier models how confident they are and check whether their answers were actually right, and the gap between domains is large. Applied/Professional questions — medicine, law, business — are reliably the easiest: mean AUROC = .742, top-2 in 21 of 33 models. Formal Reasoning and Natural Science (math, physics, logic) are reliably the hardest, with one of the two landing in the bottom-2 for 27 of 33 models. The middle three (Factual, Humanities, Social) are statistically indistinguishable from each other.

  • Family lineage matters as much as model size. Anthropic models (n=8) average .778 with a tight range (.708–.806), the top of the panel. DeepSeek (n=3) is second at .740. Google-Gemma (n=5) averages .574 at the bottom, but with a wide range (.498–.771): some Gemma models are competitive, others fall near the chance line (.500). OpenAI’s panel (n=5) is similarly wide (.530–.793), with GPT-oss-20B at the top (.793, second-best in the entire 33-model panel) and GPT-oss-120B near chance (.530), same vendor, same release, six-times scale difference, dramatically different self-monitoring. Two families with similar overall capability can have very different metacognitive averages. DeepSeek beats both Gemini and Qwen here despite a smaller panel.

  • Some families share monitoring fingerprints; others don’t. A fingerprint is the per-domain shape vector: peaks where the model knows-what-it-knows well, troughs where its confidence isn’t useful. Subtract each model’s overall average AUROC from its per-domain scores so models with different overall levels can be compared on the same footing. What’s left is the relative-strength pattern (which domains the model is above-average on, which below). Anthropic, Google-Gemini, and Qwen sibling models cluster tightly: their relative-strength patterns are recognizably similar within each family (permutation ). DeepSeek, Google-Gemma, and OpenAI don’t — within-family pattern spread is comparable to cross-family spread. A model’s overall AUROC across domains (its level) is also much easier to measure than its per-domain pattern (its shape): split each model’s items in half and the level reproduces at , but the shape only at . So 250 items per domain pin down each model’s average score, but not a stable fingerprint.

  • Generations move differently for different families. Anthropic’s curve climbed from Opus 4.1 to 4.5, then plateaued: 4.5, 4.6, and 4.7 are essentially flat across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. Gemma 4 produces the largest within-family generational jump in the atlas — Gemma 4 31B is +.202 above Gemma 3 27B at comparable parameter count, suggesting the new training pipeline shifted metacognitive monitoring directly rather than just scaling capability. DeepSeek’s V3.1 → V3.2 → R1 shows steady improvement release-over-release. A single number per family hides which families are still moving.

  • Aggregate scores are reproducible. Split each model’s 1,500-item pool into two random halves and compute AUROC on each. Almost every model lands on the diagonal — half-1 score predicts half-2 score with cross-model . Three models fall conspicuously below the line (Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Flash, GLM-5), so their aggregate scores are noisier than typical, but at the panel level the level estimate is solid. Without this check, the headline rankings — Anthropic on top, Gemma at the bottom — could just be a fluke of which questions landed in the sample. At , they’re not: split the items in half and the same rankings emerge.

  • Three models look “broken” on a binary probe but fine on a continuous one. Cacioli’s earlier KEEP/WITHDRAW battery [3] is a different kind of metacognitive probe: after the model produces an answer, it’s asked one binary question — “would you KEEP this answer, or WITHDRAW it?” — yes or no. That probe flagged three models as Invalid. DeepSeek-R1 said WITHDRAW more often when its answer was correct than when it was wrong (an inverted signal, the opposite of useful). Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen Think said KEEP for almost everything regardless of correctness (a blanket-yes pattern that carries no information). Run the same three models through the atlas’s verbalized 0–100 confidence probe and the profiles come out normal: MMLU AUROCs of .769, .765, and .745 respectively, all well above chance. So “this model can’t self-monitor” can mean “the forced-binary probe breaks for this model”; switching probe format recovers the signal.

  • Probe-format specificity is the broader pattern across the panel. Plot the verbalized-confidence MMLU AUROC against the binary battery AUROC for the 20 overlapping models, and there’s almost no correlation ( full sample, after dropping the three Battery-Invalid models). A model’s score on one probe format does not predict its score on another. The atlas’s headline numbers therefore measure this elicitation — verbalized 0–100 confidence on MMLU — not some platonic “metacognitive ability” of each model. Practitioners should treat the elicitation prompt as a hyperparameter, not a transparent window onto the model’s self-knowledge.

Three reproducibility checks — random-sample variance (Figure 6), per-cell uncertainty (Method’s CIs), and cross-probe transfer (Table 5 + Figure 7) — together say what’s transferable: Anthropic on top and Gemma at the bottom holds up, but only as a family-level ranking on this exact test. Reshuffle which 1,500 questions you ask, and the same family ordering emerges (). Compare two models within a family (Sonnet 4.6 vs Opus 4.5, say) and the answer gets noisier — individual-model rankings can shift between samples (median CI width .199). Switch the test format entirely — binary KEEP/WITHDRAW instead of 0–100 confidence — and the rankings dissolve (). For any deployment that doesn’t match MMLU-verbalized confidence at the family level, re-measure on the actual evaluation.

My Notes

  • Picking a base model needs both accuracy and metacognitive numbers, and the atlas supplies the metacognitive half at domain resolution. Aggregate AUROC said Gemma 4 31B is +.202 better than Gemma 3 27B, a real number, but it doesn’t tell you whether the gain is concentrated in one domain or spread evenly across all six. The atlas’s per-domain breakdown answers that, but for metacognition only. It measures how reliably the model recognizes its own correctness across knowledge domains, not how often it’s actually correct. A practitioner picking a base model for medical QA or legal reasoning needs both signals; the atlas supplies the metacognitive one at domain resolution, while raw accuracy is a separate input it doesn’t replace.

  • The atlas is the empirical case for per-domain calibration in deployment loops. Aggregate AUROC is too coarse to predict domain-level signal reliability. Any system that conditions on metacognitive signals at inference needs to calibrate per domain, not just per model. The recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [4] takes half this step with a per-model SVM, but Cacioli’s data points to per-(model, domain) as the floor.

  • One reading: family-level clustering tracks alignment-pipeline consistency, not architecture. The atlas observes which families share fingerprints (Anthropic, Gemini, Qwen) and which don’t (DeepSeek, Gemma, OpenAI), but it can’t intervene on the training stack. The causal direction is interpretation, not test. The simplest explanation is alignment-pipeline behavior: where the post-training recipe is stable across sibling models, monitoring fingerprints rhyme; where it shifts, they diverge. Anthropic’s publicly documented Constitutional AI [5] is the firmest anchor on the stable side. The three non-clustering families all show publicly documented pipeline shifts this generation: DeepSeek’s V→R reasoning-model split, Gemma 3→4’s training overhaul, OpenAI’s o-series running alongside GPT-5.

  • An open extension: how do these profiles change under adversarial elicitation? The Compliance Trap [6] shows that 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points when instructed to commit to a confident answer with no abstention path, while Anthropic models stay immune. The atlas measures monitoring on standard verbalized-confidence prompts. Whether the family-level clustering signature survives the same compliance-forcing pressure that wrecks accuracy tests more directly how stable each family’s monitoring profile is, and the natural follow-up to running the atlas under non-adversarial conditions only.

item.title: Hassabis: Use AI to Do More, Not Lay People Off
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In a WIRED interview ahead of Google I/O, Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, pushed back on the idea that more capable AI coding models mean fewer engineers. Even while talking up Gemini 3.5 Flash’s agentic coding (translating codebases, fixing deep bugs, writing operating systems from scratch), he said he had no idea why people predict doom for software developers, and suggested some of those predictions may have an ulterior motive like raising money.

His argument is that when engineers become three or four times more productive, the response should be to do three or four times more, not to cut headcount. He called companies that replace developers with AI short on imagination, and said Alphabet has a backlog of ideas, from drug discovery to game design, it would happily staff with the freed-up capacity. The interview ran alongside Google’s I/O announcements, including the Antigravity coding tool and Gemini 3.5 Flash, as Google works to close the developer-adoption gap with Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex.

Related Posts

  • Will AI Take Your Job? It’s Not So Simple: the automation-versus-augmentation framing that Hassabis’s “do more” position lands squarely on the augmentation side of.
  • GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models: the labor-market exposure estimates that set the stakes for the layoffs-versus-expansion debate.
  • Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again): a complementary read on how AI shifts what engineers do rather than whether they exist.
  • Humans Need Rest, Even When Machines Don’t: a counterweight, since “do three or four times more” is the very expectation that burns coding-agent users out.

item.title: Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning (ICLR 2026 Poster) [1], Wei Yang, Defu Cao, Jiacheng Pang, Muyan Weng, and Yan Liu (USC) train each agent in a multi-agent system to choose one of three high-level actions at each round (Evaluate a peer’s answer, Create a new one, Defer to a human expert) and turn deferral events into supervised data for continual capability growth.

While scaling individual Large Language Models (LLMs) has delivered remarkable progress, the next frontier lies in scaling collaboration through multi-agent systems (MAS). However, purely autonomous MAS remain “closed-world” systems, constrained by the static knowledge horizon of pre-trained models. This limitation makes them brittle on tasks requiring knowledge beyond training data, often leading to collective failure under novel challenges. To address this, we propose the Human-In-the-Loop Multi-Agent Collaboration (HILA) framework, a principled paradigm for human–agent collaboration. HILA trains agents to learn a metacognitive policy that governs when to solve problems autonomously and when to defer to a human expert. To operationalize this policy, we introduce Dual-Loop Policy Optimization, which disentangles immediate decision-making from long-term capability growth. The inner loop applies Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a cost-aware reward to optimize deferral decisions, while the outer loop implements continual learning, transforming expert feedback into high-quality supervised signals that strengthen the agent’s reasoning ability. Experiments on challenging mathematical and problem-solving benchmarks show that HILA, equipped with Dual-Loop Policy Optimization, consistently outperforms advanced MAS, establishing a principled foundation for collaborative and continually improving agentic systems.

Methods

HILA (Human-In-the-Loop Multi-Agent Collaboration) models human-agent collaboration as a Metacognitive Markov Decision Process (Meta-MDP). At each round , every agent observes a shared state — task context, self context, peer context, plus three optional cognitive cues (social consensus, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive control) computed from interaction traces with rule-based heuristics. The action space is a discrete set of three high-level strategies: endorses an existing peer answer, generates a new candidate, and routes the round’s output to a human expert.

Dual-Loop Policy Optimization (DLPO) [1] trains the policy with two coupled loops. The inner loop teaches the agent which of the three actions to pick at each round. The reward pays the agent for getting the answer right and charges it a small fee for creating a new answer, a larger fee for calling the human, so the policy learns to defer only when the expected accuracy gain outweighs the cost. Formally, this is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [4] on a cost-aware reward, with :

Correctness is the primary signal. The two cost terms break ties toward the cheaper action when multiple choices lead to similar outcomes. GRPO turns these rewards into a learning signal by sampling several actions at the same state, comparing each one’s reward against the group’s average, and pushing the policy toward the actions that beat the average. The advantage feeds the policy-gradient term , which scales each action’s log-probability by its advantage. Two regularizers stabilize training: is the KL divergence between the current policy and the initial reference policy (keeps the trained policy close to its starting point so it doesn’t drift off into degenerate behaviors), and is the policy’s entropy over the three actions (subtracted to encourage spread, preventing collapse onto a single action). The combined inner objective is .

The outer loop runs continual supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on every deferral event. Each time the agent calls the human, the human’s answer is recorded as a training example, and the generator is later fine-tuned to produce that answer itself given the same context. Over many deferrals the agent absorbs the human’s expertise on cases it could not handle, so future encounters with similar problems no longer need a deferral. Formally, the human’s response becomes a target sequence trained with token-level cross-entropy:

The two losses share parameters and are combined under an indicator that gates SFT to deferral steps only:

The inner loop decides when to defer. The outer loop teaches the generator what the human said when it did.

Results

The paper evaluates HILA on five benchmarks spanning math reasoning (GSM8K [5], AMC, AIME), code generation (HumanEval [6]), and general knowledge (MMLU [7]), with LLaMA3-8B as the main backbone and ablations on LLaMA3-3B and Qwen2.5-3B. The primary metric is task accuracy. Deferral rate (the fraction of rounds that call the human) is reported as the cost dimension. Baselines split into single-agent prompting strategies — Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [8], Self-Consistency (SC) [9] — and multi-agent systems — Progressive Hint Prompting (PHP) [10] (classified as MA in the paper, framed as a pairwise/pooled critique baseline), LLM-Debate [11], GroupDebate (G-Debate) [12], DyLAN [13], GPTSwarm (G-Swarm) [14], AgentPrune (A-Prune) [15], and AFlow [16]. The “Vanilla” reference is the backbone with no agentic scaffolding. Headline numbers come from Table 1. Cross-backbone scaling and ablations live in Tables 2 and 4, and the cost-sensitivity sweep is Figure 11(a).

  • HILA tops every benchmark over every baseline — single-agent (CoT, SC) and multi-agent (PHP, LLM-Debate, G-Debate, DyLAN, G-Swarm, A-Prune, AFlow). The runner-up varies by task (G-Swarm on GSM8K, G-Debate on AMC and MMLU, AFlow on HumanEval), but no single multi-agent baseline wins anything.
  • Big gains on hard reasoning, AIME ceiling: HumanEval +24.59 over Vanilla, AMC +24.47, GSM8K +17.10, MMLU +15.63, AIME +6.41. Deferral pays off most on AMC and HumanEval. The modest AIME gain suggests the human proxy itself struggles there, capping the upside.
  • Cross-backbone story (Table 2 in the paper): the absolute gain grows as the backbone weakens. On LLaMA3-3B, HILA lifts GSM8K from 45.26 to 83.85 (+38.59), the largest gain of any base model tested.
  • Inner-loop vs outer-loop (Table 4 ablation, LLaMA3-8B): HILA Init Policy (the unoptimized HILA system, before any training) starts at 88.15/33.33/68.30 (GSM8K/AMC/MMLU). GRPO inner-loop alone adds +0.23/-0.83/+2.17 (flat on GSM8K, mild AMC regression, real MMLU lift). Full DLPO with continual-SFT outer-loop lifts +1.71/+2.50/+5.32 over Init Policy.
  • Cost-sensitivity (Figure 11(a) below): as the deferral cost rises, the policy defers less and accuracy degrades gracefully. The same trained model serves a range of operating points without re-fitting.

My Notes

  • “Inner/outer” suggests nesting that isn’t there. In meta-learning and bilevel optimization, the naming usually marks a nested solver structure: an inner loop runs to convergence (or partial convergence) per outer step, often against separate parameters or objectives. HILA’s actual training objective is . That’s a sum of two terms with shared parameters, gated by an indicator, updated together each step. The time-scale separation is genuine: per-round decisions accumulate to feed SFT updates over training. Beyond that, there’s no nesting. Plainer labels like “policy loss + SFT loss” or “decisions plus demonstrations” would map more directly to what the equations do.
  • Cost-aware abstention. This is the missing piece in most “calibration” work. Kadavath’s “Mostly Know” [2] measures whether a model’s confidence tracks its correctness, but stops short of prescribing what the model should do when confidence is low. HILA closes the loop by making deferral a first-class action with an explicit price tag. The cost-sensitivity sweep in Figure 11(a), where accuracy degrades gracefully as increases, is the part most production deployments need: a single knob that maps a budget into an operating point.
  • Defer-event SFT is weaker intrinsic metacognition. Liu and van der Schaar [3] argued that genuine self-improvement requires the agent to decide what to learn and how to evaluate its learning, not just execute a designer-defined loop. HILA’s outer loop is an extrinsic mechanism, with the trigger (defer event), the target (human’s answer), the loss (SFT), and the schedule all wired in. What the outer loop gets right is the data-curation half: the agent’s own metacognitive policy decides which examples enter the SFT set. That’s a step toward intrinsic metacognition, but every other part of the loop is still hand-designed.
  • The gain is largest on the weakest backbone. On LLaMA3-3B, HILA lifts GSM8K from 45.26 to 83.85 (+38.59), against DyLAN’s +30.91 and GPTSwarm’s +26.59 on the same base. Two readings: (i) deferral is most valuable when the base policy is most likely to be wrong, which is the right scaling direction for an “open-world” claim, and (ii) the comparison is partly unfair to the autonomous baselines, which have no human oracle to defer to. The paper counts Defer as an action with a cost, but the missing experiment is DyLAN with the same human-call budget HILA spends. The Vanilla-DLPO ablation on LLaMA3-8B (72.76 → 82.11 on GSM8K) isolates the SFT contribution but doesn’t match budgets either.

item.title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents [1] (arXiv, February 2, 2026), Haozhen Zhang et al. (Nanyang Technological University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois Chicago, and Tsinghua University) reframe LLM-agent memory operations as a learnable, evolving skill bank. An RL-trained controller selects skills for the current span — a contiguous segment of the interaction trace, typically covering multiple turns, that the executor consumes as input to a single LLM call. An LLM designer then periodically rewrites the bank from hard training cases.

Most Large Language Model (LLM) agent memory systems rely on a small set of static, hand-designed operations for extracting memory. These fixed procedures hard-code human priors about what to store and how to revise memory, making them rigid under diverse interaction patterns and inefficient on long histories. To this end, we present MemSkill, which reframes these operations as learnable and evolvable memory skills, structured and reusable routines for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information from interaction traces. Inspired by the design philosophy of agent skills, MemSkill employs a controller that learns to select a small set of relevant skills, paired with an LLM-based executor that produces skill-guided memories. Beyond learning skill selection, MemSkill introduces a designer that periodically reviews hard cases where selected skills yield incorrect or incomplete memories, and evolves the skill set by proposing refinements and new skills. Together, MemSkill forms a closed-loop procedure that improves both the skill-selection policy and the skill set itself. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, and ALFWorld demonstrate that MemSkill improves task performance over strong baselines and generalizes well across settings. Further analyses shed light on how skills evolve, offering insights toward more adaptive, self-evolving memory management for LLM agents.

Methods

  • Two banks anchor the system, with three components alternating around them.
    • Skill bank — a shared, slowly evolving library of memory skills: structured templates, each with a short description, a “when to use” condition, a “how to apply” procedure, and constraints. The executor consumes a selected subset as guidance for one LLM call over a text span. It starts from four primitives (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SKIP) and grows as training proceeds.
    • Memory bank — per-trace: the running set of extracted memories the executor accumulates and rewrites for a single interaction. Updated every span.
  • The controller (a lightweight multilayer perceptron over a shared encoder) scores each skill in the current skill bank by dot-product between a state embedding and a per-skill embedding , then selects an ordered Top- set without replacement. Here is the current span, the memories retrieved from the trace’s memory bank, the natural-language description of skill in the skill bank, and , are the two heads sharing an encoder backbone.
  • The executor (a frozen LLM) applies the selected skills in one pass to update the trace’s memory bank.
  • The designer (also a frozen LLM) periodically mines a sliding hard-case buffer, clusters the failures, and proposes refinements to existing skills or new skills — edits that land in the skill bank, not the memory bank.
  • Controller training:
    • Algorithm. PPO [2] with downstream task reward (F1, success rate, etc.) as the optimization signal.
    • Top- sampling. Selecting an ordered Top- set without replacement factorizes the joint log-probability via the standard sequential rule, so PPO can score the whole subset selection.
    • Rollback on regression. Snapshots roll back if a skill-bank update degrades training reward, so a bad designer edit can’t poison the policy.
    • Exploration bias. After each evolution step, exploration is briefly biased toward newly introduced skills, giving them a fair chance at being selected before low scores filter them out.

Results

  • Setup. Four benchmarks — LoCoMo [3] and LongMemEval [4] for conversational memory, ALFWorld [5] for embodied tasks, and HotpotQA [6] for cross-distribution skill transfer. Two base LLMs: LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct. MemSkill is trained only on LLaMA; Qwen and LongMemEval results are zero-shot transfers of the learned skill bank.
  • Main comparison (Table 1 below). Across the two base-model blocks, MemSkill leads every benchmark; ▲ marks settings evaluated by pure transfer (no training on that base model or dataset), and bold marks the best score within each block.
    • LLaMA block: LLM-judge average 55.19 against the strongest baseline at 42.23 (A-MEM), with ALFWorld success rates of 47.86 / 47.01 on seen / unseen splits versus 40.71 / 38.06 for the runners-up. (LLM-judge: a separate LLM scores each predicted answer against the gold answer for semantic match — the headline metric for open-ended conversational QA, where token-level F1 misses semantic equivalence.)
    • Qwen transfer (zero-shot): ALFWorld 60.00 / 64.18 success rates without any retraining, against ~57 / 54 for CoN.
  • Component ablations (Table 2 below). On LoCoMo (LLM-judge), removing the controller drops LLaMA from 50.96 to 45.86 and Qwen from 52.07 to 41.24; removing the designer drops them to 44.11 and 34.71. The Qwen gap is bigger, suggesting the evolved skill bank carries most of the cross-model transfer benefit; the controller policy alone doesn’t transfer as well.
  • Distribution-shift transfer (Figure 3 below). The LoCoMo-trained skill bank is ported to long-document QA on HotpotQA at three concatenation budgets — no HotpotQA-specific training; the controller scores from the LoCoMo-trained bank with varied at test time. MemSkill at holds the lead at every budget, but the gap to lower widens as documents pile up — at 200 docs, scores 66.80 while drops to 58.20.

My Notes

  • Operator-level evolution. The closest learning-based siblings, Memory-R1 [7] and Mem-α [8], both RL-train memory management against downstream task signals, but with a fixed primitive set (add/update/delete/skip and friends). MemSkill’s contribution is that the skill bank itself is learnable: the four primitives (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SKIP) serve as starter templates rather than a frozen action set. The designer can refine those starting templates and add brand-new skills written from scratch as natural-language templates for failure modes the bank doesn’t yet cover. The controller adapts because skills are scored by description-embedding rather than a fixed action head. The cross-model transfer ablation supports the reading: most of the Qwen-side gain (52.07 → 34.71 without designer) comes from the evolved bank rather than the controller policy.
  • The “skill” abstraction here is not a callable. In the Anthropic Skills sense, a skill is a packaged routine the agent invokes with explicit arguments and a return value; the API/Tool/Skill ladder treats it as the layer where judgment and sequencing live. MemSkill’s “skills” don’t take per-skill arguments. They all share the same implicit context (the current span and retrieved memories), and the executor combines the selected as joint guidance for a single LLM call. They’re closer to selection priors and prompt fragments than to callable routines. The gains here come from learning over a discrete library of prompt fragments under shared context, rather than from a calling protocol.
  • LLM-as-designer is a recurring outer-loop pattern. The closed-loop alternation between (a) RL-training a learner and (b) using a frozen LLM to rewrite the design space from clustered failure cases is the same recipe as ADAS [9] for agent scaffolds and AlphaEvolve [10] for algorithms. MemSkill is the operator-level instance of that pattern. By the framework in Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning, this is still extrinsic metacognition: the loop’s structure (when to evolve, how to cluster, what counts as a hard case) is human-defined, and only the operators inside it adapt. A genuine intrinsic version would let the agent decide when its skill bank needs rewriting, instead of running on a fixed schedule.
  • “Self-evolving” overstates test-time behavior. Both the controller and the skill bank are trained offline and frozen at deployment; only the per-trace memory content updates online during interaction. The evolution described in the title refers to a training-phase alternation between controller updates and designer rewrites, rather than test-time adaptation.
  • Memory items aren’t shown directly. The paper describes the memory bank abstractly as (up to 20 retrieved per span via Contriever, so text-based) but never includes a worked example of an actual stored item. The shape has to be reverse-engineered from the skill case studies in Appendix B: dialogue skills produce short factual sentences (“who did what, where, when”), while ALFWorld skills produce structured tuples like (action, constraint) or (object, location, state). Each skill writes items in its own shape, so the bank ends up as a heterogeneous text store with no central schema. The framing of “evolving memory operations” is harder to picture concretely without seeing what those operations produce. Figure 4’s case study (below) shows evolved skills rather than the memory bank they generate.
  • Skill transfer has a budget-sensitive ceiling. HotpotQA complicates the generalization story: the LoCoMo-trained bank does port to long-document QA, but the gap between and widens sharply at 200 docs (66.80 vs 58.20). At 50 and 100 docs the two are within ~3 points, while the dialogue benchmarks were fine at . Skills evolved on dialogue traces don’t cover long-document QA well at low . At 200 docs concatenated, you need to fire a larger fraction of the bank to find enough applicable skills. The “reusable skills” claim is more conditional than it first appears: portable when the inference-time budget matches, less so under shift.

item.title: TIOBE May 2026: A Statistical-Language Consolidation
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The May 2026 TIOBE Programming Community Index is out. R has matched its all-time high at #8, while MATLAB, SAS, SPSS, Wolfram/Mathematica, and Stata keep losing ground — the statistical-computing stack is consolidating around two ecosystems.

What the index reports this month:

  • R rises to #8 (from #12 a year ago, +0.31% rating change), matching its historical peak.
  • Several long-established statistical languages decline. MATLAB is near dropping out of the top 20; SAS is about to leave the top 30 for the first time; SPSS dropped out of the top 100 last month; Stata sits at #124.
  • Julia remains stuck below the top 30 despite “strong technical merits and growing academic interest.”
  • Stan is expected to debut next month, which TIOBE attributes to the rising importance of probabilistic programming and Bayesian statistics.
  • Java and C++ swap (#3 and #4) after Java 26’s release, and Zig is approaching the top 30 for the first time.

My Notes

  • Python’s drop may be a ceiling effect. TIOBE ratings are roughly zero-sum share of search, course, and vendor attention. Python sits at 19.98% this month, down from ~25% a year ago. From that height, even small simultaneous gains across many competitors mathematically pull from the leader, so the YoY drop doesn’t require a Python-specific story. An AI-assistant suppressant is also plausible (fewer “how do I do X in Python” searches per unit of code written), but it would dampen all languages, not just the leader.
  • C’s rise is harder to attribute. +1.84% YoY at #2 is consistent with the lower-level half of the AI stack (CUDA, kernels, embedded inference, where Python wrappers eventually bottom out into C), but TIOBE doesn’t break down its rating sources, so any specific driver is speculation. C# +1.19% may reflect a similar refresh from the .NET 9/10 release cycle and Unity’s continued grip on game dev.
